title: Changes in Patient Volume and Care Processes at a Central Emergency Department: A Quantitative Analysis of Routine Data with Subgroup Analysis of Cardiological and Cardiac Emergencies
summary:
This study is a retrospective quantitative analysis of routine data from a central A&E department. The aim of the project is to systematically describe care processes in the central A&E department on the basis of routine data. Furthermore, differences in key process indicators are analysed in relation to the referral route, selected patient characteristics and clinical subgroups. The chosen study design allows for the investigation of real-world care processes without influencing patient care.
Emergency departments are characterised by high patient volumes, which go hand in hand with an increased workload and situations of overload. Key figures such as the length of stay in A&E (LOS) are used internationally as indicators of care processes and resource utilisation. Routine data from A&E departments offer the opportunity to systematically map such processes. Whilst previous studies have primarily described temporal trends and descriptive developments, comparative analyses of care processes depending on the referral route are as yet limited. The aim of the study is to describe patterns in care processes within the ED and to analyse differences in key process indicators depending on the referral route, selected patient characteristics and clinical subgroups.
The analysis is based on routine data from the documentation in the Patient Data Management System (PDMS, COPRA) of the ED at Düsseldorf University Hospital. The study includes all patient cases (aged 18 and over) treated in the ED between January 2023 and December 2025. The study period ensures a sufficient number of cases and a stable representation of care processes.
The study examines, amongst other things, the length of stay in the ED (LOS), the time taken until the first contact with a doctor, the initial assessment of the urgency of care, and admission decisions. The route of referral (self-presentation versus ambulance service) is the key variable for comparison. In addition, descriptive subgroup analyses are carried out for emergency patients with cardiological or cardiac conditions. The statistical analyses are descriptive and exploratory in nature; no causal conclusions are intended
